title: Channa and Kanthaka
hook: the charioteer and the white horse ride out at midnight through the city gate

segments.voice: Yesterday, one look back: the prince in the doorway, not waking Yasodhara and the baby. Your line was the hardest leaving is quiet. Did you let a goodbye last a moment longer? Day thirty-eight.
screen: `ONE LOOK BACK — THE HARDEST LEAVING IS QUIET.`

segments.voice: Who drove you to the airport the first time you really left home? Who sat in the waiting room with you, or helped carry the boxes up three flights of stairs? Most big journeys in a life have someone at the very start of them, someone who doesn't come all the way, but gets you out the door. The prince has one too. Two, in fact. It's midnight. The palace is asleep. In the stable courtyard, his charioteer, Channa, is holding the reins of a great white horse named Kanthaka. The prince swings up into the saddle. Channa takes hold of the horse's tail. And the three of them head for the city gate. Today, Channa and Kanthaka.
screen: `WHO DROVE YOU TO THE AIRPORT?` → `MIDNIGHT IN THE STABLE YARD.` → `THREE HEAD FOR THE GATE.`

segments.voice: The later telling makes this ride glow. Kanthaka is enormous and pure white, and the tradition says both he and Channa were born on the very same day as the prince. So this is no hired driver and borrowed horse. These are the companions of his whole life. The telling says the gods muffled the sound of Kanthaka's hooves with their hands so no one would wake. The city gate, so heavy it took many men to open, swung open by itself. And at the gate, a figure appears in the air: Mara, the tempter. Turn back, he says. In seven days, you'll be king of the whole world. The prince doesn't even slow down. Mara will be back in this story, and he's patient. But tonight the three ride on, and by dawn, the telling says, they've crossed three kingdoms. Now step back from the wonders for a moment. Whatever you make of muffled hooves and opening gates, the heart of the scene is simple and human. The prince did not leave alone. Channa, who had answered his questions honestly on the road to the park, now helps him go, knowing it means losing him. Kanthaka carries him as far as a horse can. Every tradition of the story keeps them, and Buddhists remember them with real affection. Great journeys are often told as solo adventures. This one isn't. The going forth, the most famous departure in Buddhism, begins with a friend holding a horse's tail in the dark.
screen: `BORN ON THE SAME DAY AS HIM.` · `MUFFLED HOOVES, AN OPEN GATE.` · `MARA OFFERS THE WORLD.` · `HE DID NOT LEAVE ALONE.` · then, large: `SOMEONE RODE WITH YOU.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the breath settle. Think of someone who got you somewhere. A parent who drove you to your first job. A friend who talked you into applying. A teacher who opened a door, a stranger who gave you directions when you were lost. Picture their face. Remember the moment, the car, the room, the road. Then, silently or out loud, say thank you. If you can, decide to tell them today. If you can't, let the thanks be enough. The bell holds the time.
Channa and Kanthaka. The charioteer and the white horse, born the same day as the prince, who carried him out of the palace at midnight.
Your line: someone rode with you. Today, thank one person who got you somewhere, with a message, a call, or a word in person. Day thirty-eight.

howItsDone: Temple murals and carvings across the Buddhist world show the great departure, the prince on the white horse Kanthaka with Channa holding its tail, and some festivals reenact the ride.

fork.setup: at the city gate, a voice in the air says: turn back, and in seven days you'll rule the world. what do you do?
options: turn back and take the throne.
fork.reveal: he rides on. Mara, the tempter, will be back, but tonight the three cross three kingdoms by dawn.

original.note: Pali: the name of the prince's white horse.

trapdoor: what you thought: the prince rode off into the night alone.
what it means: a lifelong friend and a loyal horse carried him out. the great departure begins with companions.
what a scholar hears: the Nidanakatha lists Channa and Kanthaka among the seven born at the same moment as the Bodhisatta; Mara's first appearance at the gate foreshadows the night under the tree.

sources.ref: Nidanakatha (introduction to the Jataka): the great departure with Channa and Kanthaka

notes: The co-natal list (seven born at the same moment, including Channa and Kanthaka) is from the Nidanakatha; confirm.
Gods muffling the hooves, the gate opening, Mara's offer of universal rule in seven days, crossing three kingdoms by dawn: all Nidanakatha; confirm.
Mara is named briefly here; day 52 teaches Mara as the word. Confirm this foreshadowing is fine.
